conventions: Unconstrained Markowitz mean-standard deviation maths; short sales and borrowing/lending at rf are allowed; no other constraints. Units: every mu, sigma and rf in the item is a percent per year (8 means 8%); convert to decimals before computing (m_i = mu_i/100, s_i = sigma_i/100, r = rf/100). Covariance S_ij = corr_ij * s_i * s_j. Portfolio mean E = w'm, sd = sqrt(w'Sw). Frontier: for a target mean, the minimum-sd portfolio from m and S (closed form with A0 = 1'S^-1 1, B0 = 1'S^-1 m, C0 = m'S^-1 m: var(E) = (A0 E^2 - 2 B0 E + C0)/(A0 C0 - B0^2)); draw the upper (efficient) branch solid and the lower branch faint. min-variance point: w = S^-1 1 / (1'S^-1 1) (does not depend on m or rf). tangency point: w = S^-1 (m - r 1) / (1'S^-1 (m - r 1)) (w proportional to S^-1(mu - rf 1)); the CAL is the ray from (0, rf) through the tangency point, slope = Sharpe ratio (E_T - r)/sd_T. complete point: weight in the tangency portfolio y* = (E_T - r)/(A sd_T^2) with A applied to DECIMAL returns (utility E - (A/2) var); the point is (y* sd_T, r + y*(E_T - r)), on the CAL; 1 - y* is held in the risk-free asset (y* > 1 means borrowing). Plot (sigma, mu) in percent. The slider changes exactly one input (rf, A, mu[i], sigma[i] or corr[i][j] with corr[j][i] kept equal) and everything is recomputed live; the player predicts the move of the point from slider.from to slider.to. Move codes: sign of d(sigma) (right/left) and d(mu) (up/down), |d| < 1e-6 counts as zero; 'stays' = both zero. Where an item says the risk-free asset is the benchmark (active space), read mu as expected active return, sigma as tracking-error volatility (TEV), the Sharpe ratio as the information ratio, and the risk-free asset as the benchmark itself.

omitted.reason: States that optimal holdings of illiquid assets are lower (l.210-211) and that unsmoothing raises risk estimates but not means (l.101-104), but gives no volatilities or correlations; any frontier would need invented inputs.
Beta/volatility anomaly quintiles give means and Sharpe ratios (l.386-409) but no correlations; leverage-constraint story is a constrained problem outside this unconstrained engine.
The M^2 figure (l.131-160) draws a CAL, but its plotted line (slope 0.4333) is inconsistent with its own points (R_F 3%, P at 24% / 12.5%), so it cannot seed a numeric item.
No reading in the notes states the comparative static for a change in rf on the TANGENCY portfolio, so no rf-slider tangency item was made; the only rf item is the min-variance invariance (IM-5).

items.title: CAD looks better: raise its expected excess return
items.question: The CAD forecast rises from 8% to 10% (excess). Where does the optimal (maximum-Sharpe) portfolio go?

options.label: Up and slightly right: more CAD, higher expected return
options.why: The CAD now has the higher excess-return-to-marginal-risk ratio, so the optimiser adds to it (IM-5 l.533). The book already holds more CAD than the minimum-risk 85%, so each extra CAD dollar adds a little risk as well as return.

options.label: Up and to the left: more return and less risk
options.why: Less risk would need a move back toward the 85.21% minimum-risk mix; the optimiser moves further away from it, toward more CAD.

options.label: Down and to the left, toward the minimum-risk portfolio
options.why: Treats a better forecast as a reason to cut risk. The optimal portfolio uses return AND risk; only the minimum-risk portfolio ignores returns (IM-5 l.474, l.520).

options.label: Stays put: the covariance matrix did not change
options.why: That is true of the minimum-variance portfolio, not of the tangency portfolio, whose weights are proportional to S^-1 times excess returns.

items.explanation: At the optimum the ratios E_i / beta_i (equivalently E_i / MVaR_i) are equal across assets (IM-5 l.523-526). Raising the CAD's E_i breaks the equality in the CAD's favour, so the rule "add to the position with the highest excess expected return to marginal VaR" (l.533) moves weight into CAD (90.2% -> 92.0%) until the ratios re-equalise. Because the original optimum already sits to the right of the minimum-risk mix (13.98 vs 13.85 in the notes' units, l.559 / l.506), more CAD means a little more risk: the point climbs up and slightly right.
items.inputs_source: IM-5 two-currency portfolio. Expected excess returns 8% (CAD) and 5% (EUR) are stated at l.546. The notes do not print the volatilities; they are backed out of the notes' own reconstructed VaR curve for $2m CAD + x $m EUR, sqrt(27225 + 3.9x + 39200x^2) in $000 (l.424, 95% VaR, z = 1.65 as used at l.190): (1.65 x 5% x 2000)^2 = 27225 and (1.65 x 12% x 1000)^2 = 39204 ~ 39200, and the 3.9 cross term implies rho ~ 0.00006, taken as 0. With these inputs the engine reproduces the notes' 85.21% minimum-risk CAD weight (l.501) and 90.21% optimal CAD weight (l.555) exactly. rf = 0 because the notes work in expected EXCESS returns (figure y-axis, l.589). Scale note: the notes' 'volatility' row (15.62%, 13.85%, 13.98%) is the dollar standard deviation of the $3m book per $1m, i.e. exactly 3 x the per-dollar sigma plotted here (4.62%, 4.66%); the notes' Sharpe 0.551 is therefore 1/3 of the per-dollar Sharpe ratio. Rankings and directions are unaffected.

items.title: EUR looks better: raise its expected excess return

options.label: Down and to the right
options.why: A better forecast for one asset cannot lower the maximum Sharpe ratio or the optimal expected return here.

options.label: Stays put

options.label: Straight up: same weights, same risk, higher expected return

items.title: EUR gets more volatile: where is the minimum now?
items.question: EUR volatility rises from 12% to 15%. Where does the minimum-risk portfolio go?

options.label: Up and to the right: less EUR, more CAD, and a higher risk floor

items.title: Correlation turns negative: the frontier bends left
items.question: The CAD-EUR correlation falls from 0 to -0.4. Where does the minimum-risk portfolio go?

options.label: Left (and a little down): lower risk, with a larger EUR hedge
options.why: Lower correlation means more diversification, so the whole frontier bends left; the minimum holds more EUR (14.8% -> 22.6%), which costs a little expected return.

options.label: Straight left: risk falls, weights unchanged
options.why: The minimum-variance weights depend on the correlation; with a negative correlation the EUR becomes a better hedge and gets more weight, which moves the mean too.

options.label: Right: negative correlation adds risk
options.why: Reversed polarity. Correlation below 1 is what makes diversified VaR smaller than the sum of the parts (IM-5 l.92-93).

options.label: Stays: correlation does not change individual volatilities
options.why: Individual risks are unchanged, but portfolio risk depends on the cross term 2 w1 w2 rho sigma1 sigma2 (l.87).

items.explanation: Correlation sets where portfolio risk sits (IM-5 l.329): diversified VaR is below undiversified VaR whenever correlation is below 1 (l.92-93), and the cross term 2 w1 w2 rho sigma1 sigma2 (l.87) turns negative when rho < 0. items.title: CAD gets riskier: the optimum retreats
items.question: CAD volatility rises from 5% to 7%, forecasts unchanged. Where does the optimal portfolio go?

options.label: Down and to the right: less CAD, lower return, more risk, flatter CAL
options.why: The CAD's ratio of excess return to marginal VaR falls, so CAD is cut (90.2% -> 82.5%); the book loses return and, with a riskier main holding, still carries more risk.

items.title: Risk-free rate rises: does the global minimum care?
items.question: Holding the plotted expected returns fixed, the risk-free rate rises from 0% to 2%. Where does the minimum-risk portfolio go?

options.label: Nowhere: it stays exactly where it is
options.why: The global minimum depends only on the covariance matrix; neither expected returns nor the risk-free rate enter it.

options.label: Up and to the right, following the CAL
options.why: The CAL pivots (its intercept rises) and the tangency portfolio moves, but the minimum-risk portfolio is not on the CAL's calculation path.

options.label: Down and to the left
options.why: A risk-free rate cannot change the risk or return of a portfolio that holds no risk-free asset.

items.explanation: Risk management "asks only how to make the portfolio less risky, and its answer is the global minimum where all marginal VaRs are equal" (IM-5 l.628-633). Marginal VaR depends on covariances and weights only, so the global minimum ignores the risk-free rate as completely as it ignores the forecasts. In the game the CAL visibly pivots up while the minimum-risk dot does not move: portfolio management (which divides by excess return, l.637-638) reacts; risk management does not.

items.title: Managers stop being independent

slider.label: correlation of the two managers' active returns

items.question: The two managers' deviations become correlated (0 -> 0.5). Where does the best manager mix (maximum-IR portfolio) go?

options.label: Up and to the right, and the line from the benchmark gets flatter
options.why: Correlation kills part of the diversification benefit, so the mix tilts to the better manager (60/40 -> 80/20): more active return, much more TEV, and a lower combined IR (0.72 -> 0.61).

options.label: Down and to the left: the fund de-risks
options.why: Nothing lowers the managers' own TEVs; losing the diversification benefit makes the combined TEV higher, not lower.

options.label: Stays: the managers' IRs did not change
options.why: Individual IRs are unchanged, but the combined IR above either manager's came only from independence (IM-6 l.313).

items.explanation: The combined IR of 0.72 beats both managers only because "the managers' deviations [are] independent of each other" (IM-6 l.311-314; l.381). Correlating them removes part of that diversification benefit: the maximum-IR mix tilts from 60/40 toward the better manager (80/20), its TEV rises from 4.33% to 5.50%, its expected active return rises from 3.12% to 3.36%, and its IR falls to 0.61. The point moves up-right while the line from the benchmark flattens. (The 60/40 starting mix is the notes' "risk budgets proportional to information ratios", l.285, which holds for independent managers with equal TEV.)
items.inputs_source: IM-6 two-manager risk budget. Each manager's TEV is 6% and IRs are 0.60 and 0.40 (l.280); expected active return mu_i = IR_i x TEV_i = 3.6% and 2.4% (l.304-305); the managers' deviations are independent (l.313, l.381), so corr = 0. The benchmark has zero TEV and zero active return and plays the risk-free asset (l.281), so rf = 0 in this active-return plane. A = 18.03 puts the complete portfolio at the notes' 4% overall TEV (l.279): sd_C = IR_T / A = 0.7211 / 18.03 = 4.00%, which reproduces the notes' 55.5% / 37.0% / ~8% benchmark split (l.297-300, l.304).

items.title: Manager 1 gets more skilful
items.question: Manager 1's IR improves from 0.60 to 0.80 (expected active return 3.6% -> 4.8%, TEV still 6%). Where does the best manager mix go?

options.label: Up and slightly right: more risk budget to Manager 1
options.why: Risk budgets are proportional to IRs, so Manager 1's share rises from 60% to 67%; the mix earns more and, being less balanced, diversifies slightly less.

options.label: Up and to the left: better skill means less risk
options.why: A more lopsided mix of two equal-TEV managers is less diversified, so TEV edges up (4.33% -> 4.47%), not down.

options.label: Stays: allocation follows assets under management, not skill
options.why: Risk budgets are proportional to information ratios, not to AUM or expected return (IM-6 l.378-379).

items.explanation: "Risk budgets are proportional to information ratios" (IM-6 l.285, l.378). With equal 6% TEVs, the maximum-IR weights are proportional to IR_i: 0.6:0.4 becomes 0.8:0.4, i.e. 67/33. Expected active return of the mix rises from 3.12% to 4.00% and its TEV edges up from 4.33% to 4.47% because the mix is less balanced. The combined IR rises from 0.72 to 0.89 = sqrt(0.8^2 + 0.4^2).

items.title: Manager 2 catches up
items.question: Manager 2's IR improves from 0.40 to 0.60 (expected active return 2.4% -> 3.6%). Where does the best manager mix go?

options.label: Up and to the left: a 50/50 mix earns more with less TEV
options.why: Equal IRs mean equal risk budgets; the balanced mix of two independent managers diversifies best, so TEV falls while return rises.

options.label: Up and to the right
options.why: Moving toward a balanced mix of independent managers reduces TEV (4.33% -> 4.24%).

options.label: Down and to the left: money moves to the weaker manager
options.why: Manager 2 is no longer weaker; and the mix's expected active return rises (3.12% -> 3.60%).

items.explanation: Relative risk budgets follow relative IRs (IM-6 figure caption l.345-351: IR ratio 1.50 gives risk-budget ratio 1.50). When both IRs are 0.60 the ratio is 1.00 and the mix is 50/50. For two independent managers with equal TEV, 50/50 is also the minimum-TEV mix, so the point moves up (3.12% -> 3.60%) and to the left (4.33% -> 4.24%). The combined IR rises to 0.85 = 0.6 x sqrt(2).

items.title: Active risk aversion doubles

slider.label: risk aversion A (= 2 x active risk aversion lambda_A, decimal units)

items.question: The fund's active risk aversion doubles. Where does its chosen point (manager mix + benchmark) go?

options.label: Down-left along the same line, toward the benchmark: active risk halves to 2%
options.why: The IR of the manager mix is unchanged, so the line from the benchmark keeps its slope; the fund simply holds more benchmark. Desired active risk = IR / (2 lambda_A) halves.

options.label: Jumps to the pure manager mix (no benchmark)
options.why: That is lower risk aversion, not higher: holding only the managers means MORE active risk (4.33%).

options.label: Up-right along the line
options.why: Reversed: higher aversion buys less active risk.

options.label: Stays: risk aversion does not change the managers' IRs
options.why: True about the IRs (the mix is unchanged), but the SIZE of the active bet is set by risk aversion.

items.explanation: IM-4 backs risk aversion out of the IR and the desired active risk: lambda_A = IR / (2 sigma_A) (l.155-156), i.e. sigma_A = IR / (2 lambda_A). In the game's convention A = 2 lambda_A, so the complete point sits at sd = IR_T / A. Start: IR 0.7211, A = 18.03, TEV 4.00% (the IM-6 target, IM-6 l.279). Doubling lambda_A halves the active risk to 2.00% and the expected active return to 1.44%; the manager mix is untouched, so the point slides down the same line toward the benchmark (more of the fund in the benchmark, as in IM-6 l.281). Note IM-4's own units warning (l.158): the notes' lambda_A = 0.05 is in percent units; in decimal units it is 5.
items.inputs_source: IM-6 two-manager risk budget. Each manager's TEV is 6% and IRs are 0.60 and 0.40 (l.280); expected active return mu_i = IR_i x TEV_i = 3.6% and 2.4% (l.304-305); the managers' deviations are independent (l.313, l.381), so corr = 0. The benchmark has zero TEV and zero active return and plays the risk-free asset (l.281), so rf = 0 in this active-return plane. A = 18.03 puts the complete portfolio at the notes' 4% overall TEV (l.279): sd_C = IR_T / A = 0.7211 / 18.03 = 4.00%, which reproduces the notes' 55.5% / 37.0% / ~8% benchmark split (l.297-300, l.304).

items.title: A more risk-averse investor than average

slider.label: investor risk aversion A (start = gamma-bar of the average investor)

items.question: Treat the tangency portfolio as "the market". At A = gamma-bar the investor holds exactly the market. Now her risk aversion doubles. Where does her optimal point go?

options.label: Down-left along the capital market line, toward the risk-free asset
options.why: She keeps the same risky portfolio (the market) and only changes how much of it she holds: y* halves from 1 to 0.5.

options.label: Jumps to the minimum-variance portfolio
options.why: In the CAPM nobody switches risky portfolios; everyone holds the market and differs only in the amount of factor exposure (lesson 2).

options.label: Up-right: she needs more return to compensate
options.why: Confuses the individual with the equilibrium premium. A MORE risk-averse individual takes less market exposure.

options.label: Stays: everyone holds the market
options.why: Everyone holds the same RISKY portfolio, but "each investor has his own optimal exposure" to it (IM-1 l.128).

items.explanation: CAPM lessons: "each investor has his own optimal exposure of factor risk" and "the average investor holds the market" (IM-1 l.128-129; table l.196-197). With E(R_m) - R_f = gamma-bar sigma_m^2 (l.137), an investor whose A equals gamma-bar has y* = (E_m - R_f)/(gamma-bar sigma_m^2) = 1: she holds exactly the market. Doubling A halves y*, so the point slides halfway down the same line toward the risk-free asset; the risky mix (90.2% CAD / 9.8% EUR here) is unchanged. Inputs are the IM-5 two-currency universe standing in for the market (the IM-1 notes give no numbers).
items.inputs_source: IM-5 two-currency portfolio. Expected excess returns 8% (CAD) and 5% (EUR) are stated at l.546. The notes do not print the volatilities; they are backed out of the notes' own reconstructed VaR curve for $2m CAD + x $m EUR, sqrt(27225 + 3.9x + 39200x^2) in $000 (l.424, 95% VaR, z = 1.65 as used at l.190): (1.65 x 5% x 2000)^2 = 27225 and (1.65 x 12% x 1000)^2 = 39204 ~ 39200, and the 3.9 cross term implies rho ~ 0.00006, taken as 0. With these inputs the engine reproduces the notes' 85.21% minimum-risk CAD weight (l.501) and 90.21% optimal CAD weight (l.555) exactly. rf = 0 because the notes work in expected EXCESS returns (figure y-axis, l.589). Scale note: the notes' 'volatility' row (15.62%, 13.85%, 13.98%) is the dollar standard deviation of the $3m book per $1m, i.e. exactly 3 x the per-dollar sigma plotted here (4.62%, 4.66%); the notes' Sharpe 0.551 is therefore 1/3 of the per-dollar Sharpe ratio. Rankings and directions are unaffected.

items.title: The market gets more volatile, the premium does not move

slider.label: CAD volatility (%) - the market's main holding

items.question: The average investor (A = gamma-bar) holds the market. Market variance rises (CAD vol 5% -> 6%) but expected returns are left unchanged. Where does her optimal point go?

options.label: Down and to the left: she now wants less than 100% of the market
options.why: Equilibrium breaks: at the old premium the average investor is no longer willing to hold the whole market (y* falls to 0.72). The premium would have to rise for her to hold it again.

options.label: Up and to the right: riskier market, higher expected return
options.why: That is where equilibrium must END UP (the premium rises), but the slider held expected returns fixed; the investor's point itself moves down.

options.label: Straight right: same return, more risk
options.why: She does not passively absorb the extra variance; she cuts her exposure, which lowers both risk and return.

options.label: Stays: the average investor always holds the market
options.why: Only at the equilibrium premium. With the premium frozen, the identity E(R_m) - R_f = gamma-bar sigma_m^2 no longer holds.

items.explanation: E(R_m) - R_f = gamma-bar sigma_m^2 (IM-1 l.137): the premium "rises when the market becomes more volatile" (l.150-151). Freeze the premium and raise the market's variance, and the average investor's optimal holding y* = (E_m - R_f)/(gamma-bar sigma_m^2) falls below 1 (here to 0.72): the visual breaks, with her point sliding down-left off the old CAL onto a flatter one. It re-forms only when the market premium rises by gamma-bar times the change in variance. Inputs are the IM-5 two-currency universe standing in for the market.
